title: Global Arts: Build a Recycled-Paper Collage
scenes: Today we will reuse materials while arranging an image. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Sort clean paper by colour and select pieces for your picture.
Arrange pieces on cardboard before applying glue.
Stick the pieces down and explain the main image. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Compose Body-Percussion Patterns
scenes: Today we will build and repeat a rhythmic pattern. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Mark four beat spaces with dots on paper.
Choose claps and thigh taps to fill the beat spaces.
Perform the pattern twice and check for a steady pulse. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Model a Small Clay Bowl
scenes: Today we will shape a useful object from malleable material. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Roll a smooth ball of soft material.
Press a thumb gently into the centre and pinch the sides evenly.
Smooth the rim and show how the finished bowl can stand. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Rehearse a Short Classroom Drama
scenes: Today we will use voice, space and roles to tell a story. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Assign a speaker, listener and narrator for a short scene.
Practise lines with clear facial expression and turn-taking.
Act the scene once and revise a confusing gesture. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Weave a Paper Pattern
scenes: Today we will explore repeated structure through weaving. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Lay parallel paper strips on a desk as the base.
Pass one strip over then under the base strips.
Repeat the sequence and straighten the finished pattern. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Create a Safe Dance Phrase
scenes: Today we will coordinate movement with music. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Choose two safe steps that suit the chosen rhythm.
Connect them with a pause and a change of direction.
Perform the phrase twice with control and enough personal space. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Design a Community-Care Poster
scenes: Today we will use art to communicate a helpful message. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Choose one clear message about a community need.
Draw a bold image that supports the message.
Add a few large readable words and check the layout. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Compose a Soundscape
scenes: Today we will represent a place through organised sounds. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
List three sounds heard in the chosen setting.
Assign each sound to a gentle vocal or body action.
Perform the sounds in order to represent morning, afternoon or evening. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Arrange a Mini Art Gallery
scenes: Today we will share artworks with an audience. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Choose finished works and give each a title label.
Place the works where viewers can see them without crowding.
Guide visitors to observe one artwork and ask a respectful question. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Stage a Class Performance
scenes: Today we will present performance work as a team. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Agree on the order of songs, dance or drama items.
Rehearse entry, performance and respectful exit.
Present the item and thank the audience at the end. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Look Closely at an Artwork
scenes: Today we will appreciate work using evidence. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Describe visible lines, colours, textures and shapes.
Say which details help communicate the artist’s idea.
Give one evidence-based compliment and one possible improvement. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Give Feedback on Music or Dance
scenes: Today we will use evidence to discuss a performance. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Watch or listen carefully without interrupting.
Record one strength in timing, expression or teamwork.
Suggest one useful change and say how to rehearse it. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Improve an Artwork with Feedback
scenes: Today we will revise a work thoughtfully. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Read or listen to one helpful comment on the draft.
Choose one change that supports the artwork’s purpose.
Make the change and explain how the second version improved. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: creative
title: Global Arts: Reflect and Restage a Performance
scenes: Today we will strengthen performance through reflection. Our work connects with international artists and communities around the world.
Identify one timing or storytelling issue from feedback.
Rehearse a concrete change as a group.
Restage the piece and explain the difference between the two versions. Justify a revision using evidence from another world tradition.

subject: world
title: Caring for Creation
scenes: Explain purposes of human creation and ways to protect living things.
In the faith stories studied, human beings are called to care for other creatures, worship and serve God. Plants provide food and medicines; animals may provide food or help people.
Clean air, water and healthy soil support life. We show responsibility by planting trees and disposing of rubbish properly.
With your teacher, list three living things around the school and a safe way to protect each.

subject: world
title: Promises and the Call to Serve
scenes: Describe examples of God’s promises and ways believers respond to a call.
The curriculum uses stories of Abraham (Ibrahim) and Moses (Musa) when discussing God’s promises and call. Believers learn about trust, obedience, humility and service from these stories.
Responses may include prayer, helping people in need and caring for the environment. People of different faiths may explain these promises in different ways.
Retell one story of Abraham/Ibrahim or Moses/Musa respectfully using a trusted text or a teacher’s summary.

subject: world
title: Values of Answering the Call
scenes: Identify moral lessons and faith-based benefits described when people answer God’s call.

The curriculum presents believers’ views of benefits such as drawing closer to God and hopes for long life, prosperity or eternal life. These are faith teachings, not guaranteed outcomes that everyone experiences.
Shared moral lessons include obedience, sacrifice, respect, commitment and humility. Learners can demonstrate these values in everyday kindness.
In pairs, role-play showing humility, respect or sacrifice in an everyday situation.

subject: world
title: Healthy Habits, Safe Choices
scenes: Explain ways to promote personal hygiene and safety.
Personal hygiene helps us stay clean and comfortable. The curriculum lists soap, water, toothpaste, toothbrushes and nail cutters.
Wash hands with soap, brush teeth morning and night, bathe regularly, and keep clothing clean. Sharp tools are handled by an adult or under adult guidance.
Demonstrate handwashing with an adult and write four steps.

subject: world
title: Building Good Relationships
scenes: Explain behaviours that build good relationships at home, school and in the community.
Good relationships grow through respect, love, honesty, friendliness, humility and helpful behaviour. Listening and speaking kindly can prevent conflict.
When disagreements happen, we can discuss them without insults. A peaceful community is a place where people cooperate and care for one another.
Role-play a disagreement about borrowing an item and show a respectful solution.

subject: world
title: Mapping My Neighbourhood
scenes: Sketch a neighbourhood map with home, important places and main routes.
A neighbourhood map is a simple drawing that shows where places are found. Put familiar landmarks such as the market, school, clinic or police station on it.
Use lines for roads and a key to explain symbols. Simple directions such as left, right, near and opposite make a sketch easier to use.
With an adult, observe safe familiar routes and draw a sketch that does not show anyone’s private details.

subject: world
title: Land and Water in Danger
scenes: Identify problems caused by harmful uses of land and water.
Land and water support life and livelihoods. Dumping rubbish can block gutters and pollute streams.
Poorly managed mining, careless burning, sand winning or quarrying can damage land and water. We should observe environmental problems from a safe distance and report hazards to responsible adults.
Look at pictures of clean and polluted places; compare the effects on people, animals and plants.

subject: world
title: Protecting Our Land and Water
scenes: Suggest safe ways to protect land and water from damage.
We can protect land and water by using bins, planting trees, avoiding dumping in waterways, and teaching others not to pollute. Adults and authorities manage hazardous clean-up work and mining laws.
Everyone can keep school surroundings tidy and conserve water. Looking after these resources protects our future.
Plan a safe school anti-litter campaign with a poster and one action adults can help perform.

subject: world
title: Make and Care for a Garden
scenes: Explain how to make and maintain a simple garden.
A garden is a place where useful or beautiful plants are grown. Choose a suitable safe site, prepare the soil with an adult and plant seeds or seedlings.
Plants need appropriate water, light and care. We can remove weeds, observe growth and keep rubbish away from the garden.
Plant seeds in a reused pot with a teacher; observe and record their growth for a week.

subject: world
title: Sketch Our Classroom
scenes: Sketch the classroom and locate the teacher’s desk and other objects.
A classroom sketch shows where objects are located using simple shapes. Draw the classroom outline, then mark the teacher’s table (Tt), board (Bb/Wb), cupboard (C) and your seat (Me).
A label or key helps another learner read the sketch. The drawing does not need to be perfectly to scale.
Walk around the class with your teacher and make a labelled bird’s-eye-view sketch.

subject: world
title: Why We Keep Records
scenes: Mention reasons for taking and keeping records regularly.
The curriculum places record keeping alongside classroom sketching. A record is information written down for later use.
We record dates, attendance, borrowed books or plant growth to help us remember accurately and make decisions. Records should be clear, kept safely and checked when needed.
Create a simple four-day chart of classroom plant observations with your teacher.

subject: world
title: Landmarks in Our School
scenes: Make a school-compound sketch with major landmarks.
Landmarks are places or objects that help us recognise locations. On a school sketch, show buildings, the gate, play area, library or water point.
Walk around with an adult, notice where the places are relative to one another and label them. Use simple lines and symbols to make the map clear.
With permission, walk around the school, then label four safe, familiar landmarks.

subject: world
title: Proud of My Community
scenes: Explain how to show pride in and care for one’s community.
A community is a place where people live, work and help one another. We can show pride by keeping public areas clean, respecting neighbours and protecting shared facilities.
Do not damage streetlights, school walls or taps. Report serious damage to a trusted adult or responsible authority.
Identify three community facilities and plan one safe way to care for them.

subject: world
title: Learning from Sacred Writings
scenes: Explain why followers study sacred writings and oral teachings.

The curriculum names the Bible in Christianity; the Qur’an and Hadith in Islam; and sacred myths, folktales, parables and taboos in African Traditional Religion. Followers may use these teachings to learn values and guide conduct.
Learners can listen respectfully and identify messages about kindness, truth and care for others. No child has to profess another person’s faith.
Ask a trusted adult to share a short moral story from their tradition and discuss its lesson.

subject: world
title: Festivals We Celebrate
scenes: Describe celebrations of religious and traditional festivals in Ghana.

Festivals bring people together to remember events, express thanks and strengthen identity. The curriculum mentions Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha; Christmas and Easter; and traditional festivals such as Aboakyer, Hogbetsotso, Adae and Fetu Afahye.
Celebrations may include prayer, visits, music, stories and community gatherings. Details differ among communities.
Ask a family or community member about one festival and record two activities people do.

subject: world
title: Knowing and Claiming Our Rights
scenes: Identify safe, lawful ways people can seek help when their rights are denied.
Human rights protect dignity and fair treatment. The curriculum mentions speaking up, negotiation and asking institutions such as Social Welfare, CHRAJ, the police or law courts for help.
Children should first tell a trusted adult, teacher or appropriate child-protection service if they feel unsafe. Rights are exercised responsibly while respecting other people.
Role-play telling a trusted teacher about unfair treatment and asking for help.

subject: world
title: The Early Lives of Religious Leaders
scenes: Describe age-appropriate accounts of the early lives and occupations of religious leaders.

The curriculum discusses Jesus Christ, Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and a traditional religious leader such as Egya Ahor. Its occupational examples are Jesus as a carpenter, Muhammad as a businessman and Egya Ahor as a farmer.
Different communities may preserve accounts in different ways. Discuss each respectfully and check stories with reliable religious or community sources.
Use approved texts or a knowledgeable elder to learn and retell one early-life account without inventing details.

subject: world
title: Moral Lessons from Leaders
scenes: Identify and practise moral lessons from the lives of religious leaders.

The curriculum highlights honesty, patience, hard work, courage, sacrifice and perseverance as lessons associated with religious leaders. People can practise these qualities at home, in class and in the community.
A responsible leader listens and serves others. Faith traditions may teach these virtues through different stories.
Choose a virtue and act out a 30-second situation that demonstrates it.

subject: world
title: Good Manners in Our Community
scenes: Identify good manners and why communities value them.
Good manners include greeting people, speaking courteously, being honest, respecting others and showing tolerance. They make relationships peaceful and help people feel welcome.
Societal values also encourage responsibility, hard work and patriotism. We can practise good manners every day with both friends and strangers.
Make a class good-manners chart and role-play greeting, apologising and thanking.

subject: world
title: Keeping Law and Order
scenes: Explain how rules and responsible institutions support law and order.
Communities use rules and laws to protect people and property. Police and other justice institutions have responsibilities for public safety and the fair use of the law.
Lawyers help people understand and use legal processes. Citizens should obey fair rules, avoid violence and report danger appropriately.
Role-play a safe community problem and identify who should help.

subject: world
title: Honouring Ghana’s National Symbols
scenes: Demonstrate respect for important Ghanaian national symbols.
National symbols help represent Ghana’s identity and history. The curriculum names the national flag, Coat of Arms, National Anthem, National Pledge and Adinkra symbols.
We show respect by handling flags carefully and behaving respectfully during national ceremonies. Learn the meanings of symbols without damaging them.
Create a display of two national symbols and explain a respectful way to treat each.

subject: world
title: Wise Use of Energy
scenes: Explain ways to conserve electricity and other forms of energy.
Energy powers lights and many tools we use. We save electricity by switching off lights and appliances when not needed and choosing efficient bulbs where possible.
Adults should unplug or repair unsafe electrical equipment. Conserving energy reduces waste and can help families manage costs.
With an adult, make a home or classroom energy-saving checklist.

subject: world
title: Made and Grown in Ghana
scenes: Identify agricultural products produced in Ghana and explain their value.
Ghanaian agriculture provides foods and goods such as yam, cocoyam, rice, poultry and cocoa products including chocolate. Farmers and workers help supply our homes and markets.
Using and appreciating local agricultural products supports livelihoods and jobs. Eating a variety of safe local foods helps families enjoy a balanced diet.
List five products found in your local market and ask which are grown or produced in Ghana.

subject: world
title: Ghana and Its Neighbours
scenes: Describe where Ghana and its three land neighbours are located.
Ghana is in West Africa. Côte d’Ivoire is to the west, Togo to the east and Burkina Faso to the north.
To the south is the Atlantic Ocean. These directions help us read a simple regional map and understand how Ghana connects with nearby countries.
Use a printed map or globe to identify all four directions around Ghana.

subject: world
title: Discover the Computer
scenes: Identify selected computer parts and practise basic keyboard use.
A computer has parts that work together. A keyboard lets us type, a mouse helps point and select, a storage device keeps files and a power supply provides electricity.
The curriculum highlights Tab, Caps Lock and the bottom letter row. We should use devices carefully and ask an adult before inserting or removing drives.
With permission, identify Tab and Caps Lock on a keyboard and type three short words.

subject: world
title: Sharing Information
scenes: Demonstrate ways people send and receive information.
Information can be shared through letters, posters, newspapers, phone calls or text messages (SMS). The message should suit the audience and be clear and respectful.
People can ask questions to check meaning. Children should protect private details and seek adult help before communicating with unknown people online.
Role-play a polite phone conversation and write a simple class notice.

subject: world
title: Technology Helps Us Communicate
scenes: Identify benefits of communication technology and how to use it politely.
Telephones and other communication tools help people contact one another over distances. The curriculum highlights faster contact, lower travel needs and easier communication.
Handle devices carefully, keep them out of excessive heat and follow adult guidance. Speak politely on phone calls, introduce yourself and listen to the other person.
Role-play making and receiving a polite call; demonstrate safe device care.
